title: Sunday at the Majors: Why Golf's Greatest Stage Breaks Even the Best
summary: The Sunday of a major championship is the most pressure-filled day in golf. Players who have led tournaments all week suddenly make doubles. Champions are forged and dreams dissolve in the same afternoon. We explore why Major Sundays are unlike anything else in sport.
content:
Golf is a sport played largely in silence, against yourself, with hours between shots to think about what might go wrong. This is what makes it psychologically unique. And it is what makes the final round of a major championship something that breaks players who, by any objective measure, should be immune to pressure.

Jean Van de Velde at Carnoustie in 1999, standing in the Barry Burn on the 72nd hole with a three-shot lead and what seemed like an unlosable tournament. Adam Scott at Royal Lytham in 2012, four holes from his first major, before four consecutive bogeys handed the claret jug to Ernie Els. Greg Norman's collapse at the 1996 Masters, where a six-shot final round lead evaporated hole by hole while Nick Faldo played some of the best golf of his career.

These are not stories of bad golfers. They are stories of how the major championship final round is capable of doing things to the human mind that no other sporting context quite replicates.

What Makes Majors Different

The courses are set up differently — longer, faster greens, narrower fairways, rough that punishes anything other than precision. The galleries are larger, louder, more intense. The television audience is in the hundreds of millions. And the history is everywhere: Augusta National, St Andrews, Carnoustie, Pebble Beach — these are venues that carry the weight of everything that has happened on them.

A player leading a regular tour event on Sunday is playing for a trophy, money, and world ranking points. A player leading a major on Sunday is playing against time — against every player who has ever won on that course, against their own history, against what this moment could mean for the rest of their career.

The majors do not just test your golf. They test whether you can play golf when every part of your brain is telling you that this moment is different from every other moment you've experienced.

The Champions Who Did It

What distinguishes the players who have won multiple majors — Nicklaus with 18, Tiger Woods with 15, Walter Hagen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player — is not just talent. It is an ability to manage the Sunday of a major as if it were a regular round of golf. To not let the moment become larger than the shot.

Tiger Woods at his peak was remarkable for exactly this. He did not play differently on Sunday; he played the same game, executed the same process, trusted the same swing. The difference was that he trusted it when every nerve was firing and every mistake was permanent.

Why We Watch

The possibility of collapse is part of what makes major Sundays compelling viewing. The drama is real because the pressure is real, and the pressure is real because the history is real. When a player walks to the 18th green at Augusta needing a par to win the Masters, we are watching something genuinely human — a person trying to hold themselves together at the moment when everything is on the line.

Golf would be a lesser sport without its collapses. They remind us that even the best in the world are, in the end, just people.
